newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU beef talks snared by British BSE row.
newsitem.headline: EU beef talks snared by British BSE row.

text.p: European Union talks intended to restore consumer confidence in beef after the mad cow scare could be sidetracked by a row between Britain and its partners over how to eradicate the disease.

Other EU agriculture ministers were expected to give a rough ride to Britain's Douglas Hogg, who has to explain why his government decided to suspend part of a cattle cull agreed at an EU summit in Florence in June.

EU farm commissioner Franz Fischler said on arrival for Monday's talks in the southern Irish town of Killarney that Britain must fulfil the terms of the deal in order to get a worldwide ban on British beef exports lifted.

"What I have to say is very clear. If Great Britain is interested in the lifting on the ban step by step, they have to fulfil all the preconditions...Great Britain has to accept what was agreed in Florence," Fischler told reporters.
The EU Commission has insisted that it will not accept Britain's reasons for suspending the proposed slaugther of up to 147,000 cattle, agreed at the Florence talks.

Britain cites a scientific study saying there is no evidence that the cull, on top of the destruction of up to one million older cattle a year, will hasten the eradication of Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE or mad cow disease).
But Britain's EU partners, weary of a row that paralysed EU business and monopolised the Florence summit, say they are not convinced by the British argument.
Many suspect that Prime Minister John Major is bowing to pressure from right-wingers in his Conservative Party who fear that London is increasingly surrendering sovereignty to Brussels.

Major blocked dozens of EU decisions to show his displeasure at the export ban and forced the Florence summit to come up with a step-by-step plan to get it lifted. Many of his EU partners now feel he is trying to re-write that deal.
"I always try to be friendly to everyone. But they (the British) cause us problems," French Agriculture Minister Philippe Vasseur told reporters.
Asked if he was angry at Britain, Austria's Wilhelm Molterer replied: "Yes, of course. There was a solution in Florence. My position is clear. This agreement has to be held to."

The farm ministers meeting, an informal get-together that includes a visit to a model farm and an afternoon at the race track, was supposed to focus on measures to make shoppers less suspicious of beef after the BSE scare.
The EU imposed the ban on British beef after Britain said in March there was a possible link between BSE and a fatal brain-wasting disease in humans.
EU farmers say prices have fallen sharply with consumption and the ministers should devise plans to attract shoppers back to beef and defend farm incomes.
Irish farmers, who export eight out of every 10 cattle they raise, say their sales have fallen sharply and are mounting a protest outside the hotel where the talks will be held.
